summary.title: Weapons of Math Destruction
summary.one_liner: Cathy O'Neil's 2016 book explains how opaque, unregulated, scalable algorithms (WMDs) can reinforce inequality across areas such as insurance, education, advertising and policing.
keywords: how do big data models reinforce racism
takeaways: Weapons of Math Destruction (WMDs) are algorithms that are opaque, unregulated, hard to contest, and scalable, so their biases can spread widely.
Big data models in lending, insurance, education, advertising and policing can deepen poverty and discrimination, such as denying a loan based on zip code.
The book was longlisted for the 2016 National Book Award for Nonfiction and won the Euler Book Prize (awarded 2019 by the Mathematical Association of America).
Reviewers praised the clear explanation of the problem, though one noted the section on solutions is weaker than the critique of the problem.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article summarizes Cathy O'Neil's 2016 non-fiction book on the societal impact of big data algorithms. It describes the book's argument that certain mathematical models reinforce preexisting inequality across fields such as insurance, advertising, education, and policing, and defines the three features O'Neil associates with these models: opacity, lack of regulation, and difficulty to contest. The page also covers the book's reception, including praise from reviewers and its awards, and lists a long set of reviews in its references. It is a secondary overview rather than the book itself.
